title: EFFECTS OF INDOOR LIGHTING ON MOOD AND COGNITION
research_question: Does a luminous setting act as a mood inducer, and if so, will these mood valences impair or enhance ongoing cognitive processes? Specifically, how do illuminance, colour temperature, and Colour Rendering Index (CRI) interact with gender to influence mood and cognitive performance?

participants.description: Ninety-six subjects (aged 18-55) per experiment (total 192) from Sweden, randomly assigned to eight groups of 12 subjects each per experiment.
participants.recruitment: Recruited through local press and radio advertisements, paid 200 Swedish crowns (c. 30 U.S. dollars).

stimuli_or_exposures.description:
A chamber-room (3.9 m × 3.8 m × 2.5 m) furnished as an office with neutral room coloration (off-white walls/ceiling, off-white/grey floor), a big green flower, two false windows with green curtains, green writing pads, and a PC. Lighting was provided by six ceiling-mounted fluorescent luminaires, each with four lamps. 

Experiment 1: High CRI (95) lighting conditions. Two illuminance levels (300 lx 'dim' vs 1500 lx 'bright') and two colour temperatures (3000K 'warm' white vs 4000K 'cool' white).

Experiment 2: Low CRI (51 for 'warm' white, 58 for 'cool' white) lighting conditions. Two illuminance levels (300 lx 'dim' vs 1500 lx 'bright') and two colour temperatures (2950K 'warm' white vs 4200K 'cool' white).
stimuli_or_exposures.source: Environmental setting and Apparatus sections, p. 3

measures.instrument: Six general knowledge questions (recall) and 18 multiple-choice questions (recognition) about a 7-page compressed text on an ancient culture.
Embedded figure task (Smith & Broadbent, 1980) with two answer sheets, each comprising five solution figures and 16 target figures.
Recall of words from three PC-presented word-lists (16 words each) with positive, negative, and neutral affective tones.

Evaluation of a fictitious female secretary's personnel folder (neutral characteristics) using a 7-point scale across dimensions like qualifications, skills, motivation, attitude, achievement, intelligence, concern, ability to get along, promotion, and overall evaluation.
PANAS (Positive Affect Negative Effect Scales) (Watson et al., 1988), comprising 10 adjectives per emotional dimension on a 5-point scale.
Seven 5-point, unipolar items (glaring, dim, soft, bright, warm, intense, cool) to evaluate the room light.

mechanisms: Luminous milieu acts as a mood inducer, which in turn affects cognitive processes.
Mood-congruence hypothesis: subjects' memory performance is related to the valence of their mood and material to be learned.
Halo effect: a rater bias leading to an overall impression of an appraisee derived from a salient characteristic (e.g., gender).
implementation_implications: The criteria for good indoor lighting may need to be revised to account for females' and males' differential emotional and cognitive responses to lighting conditions.
Lighting design should consider the interaction between colour temperature, illuminance, CRI, and gender to optimize mood and cognitive performance.

tables.description: Mean room light evaluations and cell standard deviations on seven dimensions as a function of illuminance level (300 lx vs 1500 lx) in Experiment 1.
Mean room light evaluations and cell standard deviations on seven dimensions as a function of gender in Experiment 1.
Mean room light evaluations and cell standard deviations on seven dimensions as a function of illuminance level (300 lx vs 1500 lx) in Experiment 2.

limitations: The interpretation of the gender effect on free recall performance is problematic as females and males were equally induced in respective moods, and no interaction between gender and word-list was found, suggesting a potential mediation effect on cognitive process.
The low CRI conditions in Experiment 2 did not produce appropriate context cues to enhance long-term recall and recognition processes.

The performance appraisal task only included a female ratee, limiting the generalizability of the halo effect findings; future studies should vary both rater and ratee genders and mood valences for more conclusive data.
